idea.body: A rate compares two different kinds of quantities, like distance and time, or cost and count. A unit rate is a rate written for just one of the second quantity: how much for one minute, one item, one liter. Finding a unit rate means dividing the first quantity by the second. A drone travels 120 meters in 4 seconds. Dividing 120 by 4 gives a unit rate of 30 meters per second. Unit rates make two different rates easy to compare. Both boil down to the same per-one measure, even when the original amounts looked nothing alike.

workedExample.prompt: A rocket engine burns 180 liters of fuel in 12 seconds. A second engine burns 200 liters of fuel in 16 seconds. Which engine burns fuel at a faster rate, in liters per second?
steps: Find the first engine's unit rate: 180 divided by 12 is 15 liters per second.
Find the second engine's unit rate: 200 divided by 16 is 12.5 liters per second.
15 liters per second is more than 12.5 liters per second.
The first engine burns fuel faster.

ways.name: Divide to find the unit rate
ways.when: Use this first, since dividing straight to a per-one amount compares any two rates directly.
steps: Find the first pump's unit rate: 240 divided by 8 is 30 liters per minute.
Find the second pump's unit rate: 350 divided by 10 is 35 liters per minute.
35 liters per minute is more than 30 liters per minute.
ways.example: A pump fills 240 liters in 8 minutes. A second pump fills 350 liters in 10 minutes. Which pump fills faster, in liters per minute?
ways.answer: the second pump, 35 liters per minute
ways.trap: Dividing the time by the amount instead of the amount by the time.

ways.name: Scale a rate table
ways.when: Use this when the target amount is a clean multiple of the given rate.
steps: Write the given rate as the first row: 3 minutes to 15 boxes.
Multiply both numbers by the same amount to build equivalent rows: times 2 gives 6 minutes to 30 boxes.
Times 3 gives 9 minutes to 45 boxes, matching the 9 minutes asked for.
ways.example: A conveyor belt moves 15 boxes every 3 minutes. Scale a rate table to find boxes moved in 9 minutes.
ways.trap: Multiplying only the minutes or only the boxes, instead of both by the same amount.

figure.alt: A rate table with columns minutes and boxes: rows 3 and 15, 6 and 30, 9 and 45, each row scaled up from the first.

ways.name: Cross multiply to compare
ways.when: Use this when the numbers do not divide evenly and a decimal unit rate is messy.
steps: Write each rate as a fraction: 18 over 4, and 25 over 6.
Cross multiply: 18 times 6 is 108, and 25 times 4 is 100.
108 is bigger than 100, so 18 over 4 is the bigger rate.
ways.example: A hose fills 18 liters per 4 minutes. A second hose fills 25 liters per 6 minutes. Which fills faster, using cross multiplication?
ways.answer: the first hose, 18 liters per 4 minutes
ways.trap: Mixing up which cross product belongs to which hose's rate.
